title: Pilot closeout + next steps — Northbridge Bank (Redwood Inference)
next_steps: Redwood to send closeout recap + agreed success criteria (incl. measured numbers + test conditions) to Sarah and Mei
Northbridge to confirm preferred production topology (Redwood Private in their VPC vs Dedicated pool) after internal architecture review
Redwood Security (Naomi) to share evidence pack index + SOC 2 request instructions and answer the remaining retention/audit log questions
Redwood TAM (Liam) to provide CS handoff packet template: runbook outline, SLOs, alerting, escalation, and access checklist
Northbridge to schedule procurement intro with Nina + Legal for timeline and purchasing path (Marketplace vs direct)
body:
Fireflies.ai meeting transcript

Title: Pilot closeout + next steps — Northbridge Bank (Redwood Inference)
Date: 2025-06-10
Time: 4:03pm – 4:55pm ET
Duration: 52 min

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Rachel Kim (Enterprise CS), Liam O'Rourke (TAM), Evan Scott (Solutions Eng), Naomi Feldman (Security/Compliance)
Northbridge Banking: Sarah Patel (GenAI Platform), Tom Reynolds (InfoSec), Mei Chen (SRE/Observability), Jason Miller (Enterprise Architecture), Nina Kapoor (Vendor Mgmt)

---
Summary (auto-generated)
- Recapped pilot goals and results (latency/throughput, stability, audit logging, VPC connectivity).
- Confirmed the success criteria Northbridge cares about for production: predictable performance under peak, auditability, data boundary clarity, and operational readiness.
- Discussed production rollout plan options (Private in Northbridge VPC vs Dedicated capacity) and the security/procurement steps required.
- Agreed on CS handoff artifacts: runbook, SLO dashboard, alerting, access controls, change management, and escalation path.

Topics
1) Pilot recap + metrics
2) Security & compliance wrap-up (audit logs, retention, SSO)
3) Production architecture and rollout phases
4) CS handoff packet (runbooks / monitoring)
5) Procurement + next meetings

Action items (auto-generated)
- Rachel to send closeout recap and “success criteria confirmation” email (EOW)
- Evan to attach benchmark methodology and the exact load profile used (EOW)
- Liam to schedule SLO + runbook working session with Mei (this week)
- Naomi to follow up on remaining evidence requests and retention wording (48 hours)
- Nina to share procurement intake checklist + preferred contracting vehicle (Marketplace vs direct)

---
Transcript

[00:00] Rachel Kim: Alright, I think we’re good. Thanks everyone for making the time. This is meant to be a pilot closeout, like a recap of what we did, confirm the success criteria, and then define the handoff artifacts if we move into rollout. 

[00:15] Sarah Patel: Yep, sounds good. We’ve got like 50 minutes. 

[00:18] Rachel Kim: Perfect. Quick intros just in case — I’m Rachel, enterprise CS. Liam is our TAM on regulated accounts. Evan supported the POC on the technical side. Naomi from our security team is here for any last compliance questions.

[00:32] Tom Reynolds: Tom, InfoSec. 

[00:34] Mei Chen: Mei, SRE, I’ve been chasing the logs and the dashboards. 

[00:38] Jason Miller: Jason, architecture.

[00:40] Nina Kapoor: Nina, vendor management. I’m mostly here to understand the buying path and what you need from us.

[00:47] Rachel Kim: Great. So agenda: Evan will do a short recap of results, then we’ll go around and confirm the “did we hit the thing” criteria, then talk rollout plan and then handoff.

[01:01] Evan Scott: Cool. I’ll keep it tight. So the pilot scope as we wrote it in the mutual action plan was: (1) validate VPC connectivity and private routing, (2) validate performance under your representative workload — the customer support summarization and the internal knowledge assistant, (3) validate audit logging and export, and (4) validate SSO / SAML path for console access.

[01:22] Evan Scott: On performance: on the support summarization prompt set, with your max output cap at 512 tokens, we were seeing steady p50 end-to-end around ~750 to 900 ms, p95 around ~1.4 to 1.8 seconds. That’s with streaming enabled, so time-to-first-token was usually in the 150–250 ms range. I’ll caveat: that’s in the us-east region and with the specific model profile we pinned. 

[01:50] Sarah Patel: And that’s through our VPC endpoints, not public internet.

[01:53] Evan Scott: Correct, through the VPC path. There were a couple days with higher p95 when you had the retry loop on the client, but once we fixed that, it stabilized.

[02:03] Mei Chen: Yeah, that was us. We were double retrying. 

[02:06] Evan Scott: Right. On throughput: we ran the peak simulation, roughly 120 concurrent requests on the “assistant” endpoint, average prompt ~900 tokens input with a long system preamble. We achieved about 85–95 req/min sustained without queue blowups, and tokens/sec averaged ~2.1k across the pool. Again, depends on the exact prompt distribution.

[02:31] Jason Miller: So that meets the “don’t fall over at 9am Monday” test.

[02:34] Evan Scott: That was the intent, yeah.

[02:36] Evan Scott: On reliability: we had one incident early where you saw intermittent 429s. That was rate limit configuration mismatch. After we aligned quotas, we were stable. Uptime during the last 2 weeks of the pilot was effectively 100% from your probe, with one short blip when you rotated the NAT rules. 

[02:56] Mei Chen: That was also us.

[02:58] Evan Scott: Yep.

[03:00] Evan Scott: On audit logs: we confirmed the events you needed were present — admin logins, key changes, model version changes, API key creation/disable, role changes. And we set up export to your logging sink. There was some back-and-forth about field naming and timestamps. We sent the sample payloads.

[03:20] Tom Reynolds: The big thing for us was making sure we can answer: who accessed what, and did prompts or outputs get logged.

[03:28] Evan Scott: Right, and we were explicit: by default, we don’t log prompt/output content in audit logs. The audit logs are control-plane events. Request logs are separate and can be configured; and you can turn off body capture. Naomi can probably re-state that cleanly.

[03:44] Naomi Feldman: Yeah. The short version: audit logs are “who did what in the system,” not “what did the user say.” For content logging, we support configurable retention and redaction policies on the request/trace side depending on deployment mode. For your pilot config we kept body logging disabled and only logged metadata needed for debugging.

[04:04] Tom Reynolds: Good.

[04:06] Evan Scott: Last: SAML. We did hit the metadata validation error — that’s the ticket you opened. We fixed it with a workaround on the IdP side plus a validation patch on ours. That should be closed.

[04:19] Sarah Patel: Yeah, SAML is now working. We have two roles mapped.

[04:23] Rachel Kim: Great. Before we jump to rollout: Sarah, do you want to confirm from your side, did we meet the pilot success criteria you set at kickoff?

[04:33] Sarah Patel: Mostly yes. The big ones were: private connectivity, predictable latency under load, and “don’t give security heartburn.” We are not ready to sign anything today, but we’re aligned that technically it works.

[04:47] Rachel Kim: That’s fair.

[04:48] Sarah Patel: The remaining questions are more about: how do we operationalize this, and which deployment flavor is right — Private in our VPC versus Dedicated. 

[04:59] Jason Miller: And also what’s the long-term story if we need on-prem. Not immediate, but we get asked.

[05:05] Rachel Kim: Yup. We can cover that at a high level.

[05:08] Rachel Kim: Mei, from SRE side, did we give you enough visibility to be comfortable?

[05:14] Mei Chen: I’m like 80% there. The Redwood Console dashboards were helpful, especially token breakdown and p95. What I need for prod is: an exported metrics feed to our Prometheus / Datadog, and a clear SLO doc — like, what do we alert on, what’s normal, what’s “page someone.”

[05:33] Liam O'Rourke: That’s exactly the CS handoff packet we want to put together. For regulated pilots we usually deliver: SLOs, runbook, escalation contacts, and the “known gotchas” list. 

[05:44] Mei Chen: Also, I’d like to pin model versions and know when changes happen.

[05:49] Evan Scott: We can pin versions, and we can notify you of any changes. In Private deployments you control the rollout policy even more tightly.

[05:58] Tom Reynolds: On security, I’m okay with where we landed, but I still need two things in writing: retention defaults and where data is stored. We got close in the questionnaire but our governance team asks for very specific language.

[06:14] Naomi Feldman: Understood. And we should keep it precise — we won’t say “HIPAA compliant” or anything like that. We can say what controls exist, and what is in-scope for our SOC 2, and what you configure.

[06:26] Tom Reynolds: Yeah, please no marketing language.

[06:28] Rachel Kim: Agreed.

[06:30] Rachel Kim: Okay, so rollout plan. Sarah, how are you thinking about phases?

[06:35] Sarah Patel: Phase 1 is an internal beta: 200 users, only non-production data, with the support summarization tool. Phase 2 would be broader internal usage, and then Phase 3 is any external-facing workflow, which is where the risk committee gets involved.

[06:55] Rachel Kim: Makes sense. In Phase 1, what matters most: cost, latency, or controls?

[07:01] Sarah Patel: Controls and predictability. Cost matters but it’s not the number one right now.

[07:06] Jason Miller: And also, we don’t want to be surprised by capacity. If we do a big push and suddenly the model endpoint is slow because shared infra is busy, that’s a problem.

[07:18] Evan Scott: That’s why we’ve been talking about Dedicated or Private. Hosted is fast to start, but for your requirements, Dedicated and Private are the right options.

[07:29] Rachel Kim: Let’s talk about the two options in plain terms.

[07:32] Rachel Kim: Dedicated: you get a reserved GPU pool managed by us. Strong isolation, predictable throughput, SLA-backed. Private: we deploy into your VPC (and on-prem is possible later), you control networking, and you can integrate deeper with your KMS/HSM and logging.

[07:52] Jason Miller: Private seems closer to what our architecture board likes, but it’s heavier operationally.

[07:58] Liam O'Rourke: True, but we handle a lot of the day-two operations with you. Also, the operational model is different: for Private, you’ll have clearer boundaries for data residency and network flows, which usually makes security approvals easier.

[08:13] Tom Reynolds: Yeah, that’s the point. Our risk people like “it’s in our VPC.”

[08:17] Sarah Patel: But I also don’t want my team to become GPU operators.

[08:22] Evan Scott: You won’t be writing CUDA kernels, I promise. But you will have more knobs: update windows, how you do rollouts, and how metrics go to your systems.

[08:32] Mei Chen: My worry is: if it’s in our VPC, who’s on the hook at 2am.

[08:38] Rachel Kim: That’s why the handoff is important. We’ll define: what you monitor, what we monitor, and what the escalation path is. For most customers we do shared responsibility: you monitor your network and upstream apps; we monitor the inference runtime health and SLOs we commit to.

[08:58] Nina Kapoor: From procurement, I just need to know what I’m buying. Like: is this a SaaS, is it a license, is it Marketplace.

[09:06] Rachel Kim: For Private we can do direct contract or cloud marketplace depending on your preference. Dedicated is typically a capacity contract with an SLA. We should do a separate call with your procurement + our legal to align.

[09:22] Sarah Patel: Nina will appreciate that. 

[09:25] Nina Kapoor: I always appreciate not being surprised.

[09:27] (crosstalk)

[09:28] Rachel Kim: Okay. Before procurement, let’s lock the success criteria in writing. I’m going to read back what I have, and you tell me if it’s correct.

[09:37] Rachel Kim: 1) Private connectivity: all inference traffic stays within Northbridge-controlled network boundaries (VPC endpoint), no public egress required.

[09:46] Sarah Patel: Yes.

[09:47] Rachel Kim: 2) Performance: for the summarization workload, p95 end-to-end under 2 seconds under the tested load profile, with time-to-first-token under 300 ms, and no sustained queue growth at expected concurrency.

[10:02] Sarah Patel: That’s right, though we’ll want to word it as “under pilot conditions.”

[10:07] Evan Scott: Yep, we’ll attach the load profile doc.

[10:10] Rachel Kim: 3) Operational controls: ability to pin model versions and have controlled rollouts.

[10:18] Mei Chen: Yes.

[10:19] Rachel Kim: 4) Auditability: audit logs capture administrative actions and can be exported to Northbridge’s SIEM; prompts/outputs not captured in audit logs by default.

[10:31] Tom Reynolds: Correct, and we need the export frequency and retention options clarified.

[10:38] Naomi Feldman: We can provide that.

[10:40] Rachel Kim: 5) Identity: SAML SSO works for console access with role mapping. 

[10:47] Sarah Patel: Confirmed.

[10:49] Rachel Kim: Great.

[10:51] Rachel Kim: Now: what’s the decision point to move from pilot to Phase 1 rollout? 

[10:57] Sarah Patel: We need an internal architecture review next week, and Tom needs to close out the security questionnaire with the governance team. If those are green, we’ll request a commercial proposal.

[11:10] Nina Kapoor: And I’ll need a vendor intake packet. SOC 2, insurance, DPA, that stuff.

[11:16] Naomi Feldman: Understood. We have an evidence pack index that makes it easier. SOC 2 is available under NDA and controlled sharing. We can also provide our standard security overview and data flow diagrams.

[11:27] Tom Reynolds: That’s the other thing: the diagram. Our team asked “where is the control plane” and “what metadata leaves the VPC.”

[11:36] Naomi Feldman: For Private, we can be very explicit: data plane stays in your VPC; control plane interactions are limited and can be configured. For the pilot we used a standard pattern; we can document the exact endpoints.

[11:51] Jason Miller: That’s important. If anything crosses out, we need to justify.

[11:55] Naomi Feldman: Yep. We’ll provide the details and avoid over-claims.

[12:00] Rachel Kim: Okay, let’s shift to CS handoff artifacts. If we assume you move into Phase 1, what do you need from us to feel operationally ready?

[12:10] Mei Chen: Runbook. Like real runbook. Not just “restart service.” I want: common alerts, what they mean, what logs to look at, escalation steps, and how to tell if it’s us or you.

[12:25] Liam O'Rourke: Perfect. Our standard package includes:
- Runbook (deployment overview, health checks, common failure modes)
- SLO doc (latency, error rate, availability targets)
- Dashboard links (Console + exported metrics)
- Alerting recommendations (thresholds and burn-rate if you do it that way)
- Escalation policy (support SLAs, who to page)
- Change management plan (how updates/rollouts happen)

[12:50] Mei Chen: That list is good.

[12:52] Sarah Patel: Also a “how to onboard new teams” doc. We’ll have other groups wanting access.

[12:58] Rachel Kim: Great point. We can include access and RBAC guidelines: which roles, how to request API keys, how to do least-privilege.

[13:08] Tom Reynolds: I’ll add: audit evidence. Like, not the SOC report itself, but “here are the log fields and where they go.”

[13:16] Evan Scott: We have the audit log schema sample. Some of the field names are a bit… I don’t love them, but they’re stable. 

[13:26] Mei Chen: As long as it’s consistent.

[13:28] Rachel Kim: We can put the schema into the handoff pack and link to the example config we used.

[13:35] Rachel Kim: On SLOs: during pilot you were watching p95 and error rate. Do you want a formal SLO like 99.9 and p95 under X?

[13:46] Sarah Patel: For Phase 1, yes but maybe a bit looser. For Phase 2, we’ll tighten.

[13:52] Mei Chen: I’d rather not commit to p95 under 1 second until we see real traffic. But we can set a target.

[14:00] Liam O'Rourke: That’s normal. We can define an “internal objective” and a separate “contractual SLA.”

[14:06] Nina Kapoor: Please keep those words straight in the proposal.

[14:09] Rachel Kim: Yes.

[14:11] Rachel Kim: Let’s talk about monitoring integration: would you prefer we push metrics to you, or you pull?

[14:17] Mei Chen: Pull is easier. But if you have a supported exporter, we’ll take it.

[14:22] Evan Scott: We can expose metrics endpoints in Private. For Dedicated/Hosted we can provide an integration via our APIs and webhooks. In your case, Private makes it clean.

[14:35] Jason Miller: We’re leaning Private, but we want the commercial and operational differences spelled out.

[14:41] Rachel Kim: We can do that: a one-pager that compares Dedicated vs Private for regulated. Not marketing-y, just facts.

[14:50] Sarah Patel: Please.

[14:52] Rachel Kim: Now, open issues. I have two: audit log export format questions, and retention language. Anything else?

[15:00] Tom Reynolds: One more: incident notification timelines. Who tells us if you have an incident.

[15:06] Liam O'Rourke: We have standard incident communications and can align on your requirements. For enterprise, we provide an incident process document and escalation contacts.

[15:14] Tom Reynolds: Okay.

[15:16] Sarah Patel: And we’ll want a named support channel. We don’t want to go through generic.

[15:22] Rachel Kim: Understood. If we move forward, you’ll have a named TAM (Liam) and a support queue with enterprise SLA.

[15:31] Nina Kapoor: I’m going to ask about pricing, but I know this isn’t the pricing call.

[15:35] Rachel Kim: Right, we won’t do pricing live. But we can outline the structure: Dedicated is reserved capacity; Private is platform fee plus support tier, and then capacity depending on topology. We’ll send a proposal once you confirm deployment preference.

[15:52] Sarah Patel: That’s fine.

[15:54] Rachel Kim: Evan, can you summarize the “methodology” part you’ll send? Just so it’s clear.

[16:00] Evan Scott: Yeah. I’ll send a short doc: model version, quant profile, max tokens, streaming on/off, concurrency, prompt length distribution. Because if you rerun the test with different prompts you’ll get different numbers, and we don’t want confusion.

[16:18] Mei Chen: Please include the client timeouts, too. That bit us.

[16:21] Evan Scott: Yep.

[16:23] Rachel Kim: Naomi, what’s your plan on the security write-up?

[16:28] Naomi Feldman: I’ll send the evidence pack index link and then a short note answering the remaining questions: retention defaults by deployment mode, what’s configurable, and the audit log vs request log distinction. For SOC 2, we’ll do controlled share once Nina sends NDA requirements.

[16:46] Nina Kapoor: Our NDA is standard. I can send it today.

[16:49] Naomi Feldman: Great.

[16:50] Rachel Kim: Okay. Sarah, do you want to talk about long-term on-prem? Just to make sure we’re aligned.

[16:56] Sarah Patel: Just high level: we have a couple workloads that may go on-prem eventually. Not this year. But we don’t want to choose a vendor that can never do it.

[17:07] Evan Scott: Understood. Our Private offering includes an on-prem option for regulated or air-gapped environments, but it’s a different rollout. For now we’d focus on VPC.

[17:18] Jason Miller: That’s enough for the board.

[17:21] Rachel Kim: Good.

[17:23] Rachel Kim: Let’s do a quick round: what would stop this from moving forward?

[17:29] Sarah Patel: For me: if the architecture review decides the control plane story is messy.

[17:35] Tom Reynolds: If we can’t get crisp answers on retention and data flow. Or if someone tries to oversell compliance.

[17:42] Mei Chen: If we can’t get metrics into our stack and have a clear “who owns what.”

[17:48] Nina Kapoor: If contracting takes 6 months. We need a path that fits our procurement process.

[17:55] Rachel Kim: All reasonable.

[17:57] Liam O'Rourke: On procurement: sometimes Marketplace can speed it up if you already have that channel. If not, direct can be fine. We’ll follow your lead.

[18:06] Nina Kapoor: We do have AWS Marketplace for some vendors. I need to check if this fits.

[18:12] Rachel Kim: Great.

[18:13] Rachel Kim: Let’s define the CS handoff artifacts more concretely. I’ll propose a checklist and you tell me if anything’s missing.

[18:21] Rachel Kim: Handoff packet v1:
1) Architecture diagram (VPC topology, endpoints, key integrations)
2) Access & RBAC guide (SAML roles, API keys, break-glass)
3) SLO/SLA definitions (targets + measurement method)
4) Dashboard links (Redwood Console + external metrics)
5) Alerting playbook (thresholds, recommended alerts)
6) Incident & escalation process (contacts, severity levels)
7) Runbook (common issues, troubleshooting)
8) Change management (release notes, maintenance windows)
9) Security appendix (audit log schema, retention configuration summary)

[18:58] Mei Chen: Add “capacity planning” — how do we know when to scale.

[19:02] Evan Scott: Good call. We can include scaling signals: queue depth, tokens/sec saturation, GPU utilization (where visible), and recommended headroom.

[19:12] Sarah Patel: And “rollout plan.” Like, step-by-step.

[19:16] Liam O'Rourke: Yep, we’ll include a phased rollout template.

[19:20] Tom Reynolds: Also include how you handle model updates. If you change kernels or whatever, we need notice.

[19:28] Evan Scott: For Private, you can pin, and updates are controlled. For Dedicated, we provide change windows and release notes. We’ll document both.

[19:39] Rachel Kim: Great.

[19:41] Rachel Kim: Mei, would you be up for a 30-minute working session with Liam this week to align on SLOs and monitoring?

[19:48] Mei Chen: Yes, Thursday afternoon ideally.

[19:51] Liam O'Rourke: I can do Thursday 2 ET.

[19:54] Mei Chen: Works.

[19:55] Rachel Kim: Perfect.

[19:57] Rachel Kim: Sarah, for architecture review next week, what materials do you need from us?

[20:03] Sarah Patel: The data flow diagram, and the Dedicated vs Private comparison. And a short deck slide on results.

[20:11] Rachel Kim: We’ll send a concise pack.

[20:13] Rachel Kim: Tom, anything else you need besides the retention language and evidence index?

[20:19] Tom Reynolds: I might need a call with Naomi to walk through a couple of the questions. Our team sometimes misreads the answers.

[20:26] Naomi Feldman: Happy to do that. Maybe early next week.

[20:30] Rachel Kim: Great.

[20:32] Nina Kapoor: For me, I need: legal entity name, where you’re hosting, and if you have standard terms. And the insurance cert.

[20:40] Rachel Kim: We’ll coordinate with our legal team once you’re ready to start procurement. But I can send the basics in the recap.

[20:48] Sarah Patel: Okay.

[20:50] Rachel Kim: Quick note: we appreciated the feedback during the pilot. The SAML issue was helpful to surface. We’ve already applied a fix so it won’t happen again.

[20:58] Sarah Patel: Yeah, that was painful for a day.

[21:01] Evan Scott: Sorry about that. The metadata file had an extra whitespace— it was silly.

[21:05] Mei Chen: It always is.

[21:07] (laughter)

[21:08] Rachel Kim: Alright. Before we wrap, let’s make sure next steps are explicit.

[21:13] Rachel Kim: 1) Rachel sends recap email confirming success criteria + results, and attaches the handoff checklist.

[21:20] Rachel Kim: 2) Evan sends benchmark methodology doc.

[21:23] Rachel Kim: 3) Naomi sends evidence pack index + retention/audit language follow-up.

[21:28] Rachel Kim: 4) Liam + Mei monitoring/SLO working session Thursday 2 ET.

[21:33] Rachel Kim: 5) Sarah schedules/does architecture review next week; we provide diagram + Dedicated vs Private comparison.

[21:41] Rachel Kim: 6) Nina sends procurement intake requirements and indicates whether Marketplace is an option.

[21:48] Nina Kapoor: Yep.

[21:50] Sarah Patel: Also: we’ll tell you if the review is green by end of next week.

[21:56] Rachel Kim: Perfect.

[21:57] Tom Reynolds: Naomi, can you also include incident response details. Like, do you have an IR plan.

[22:03] Naomi Feldman: Yes. We can provide our incident response overview and how we notify customers. Some details are in the evidence pack.

[22:10] Tom Reynolds: Great.

[22:12] Rachel Kim: Anything else before we give you time back?

[22:15] Jason Miller: One question: if we go Private, can we keep everything in a single region.

[22:21] Evan Scott: Yes. You can choose regional isolation. Multi-region is optional, but single-region is supported and common for regulated.

[22:28] Jason Miller: Good.

[22:30] Sarah Patel: Another question: we had some stakeholders ask “why not Bedrock.” We’re going to have to answer that.

[22:37] Rachel Kim: Understood. Not to do a battlecard here, but the short answer is: predictable performance and operational tooling, plus deployment flexibility. We can provide a neutral comparison if helpful.

[22:49] Sarah Patel: That’s helpful. 

[22:52] Rachel Kim: Okay. Thanks everyone. We’ll follow up with materials. 

[23:00] Sarah Patel: Thanks, talk soon.

[23:02] Mei Chen: Thanks.

[23:03] Tom Reynolds: Thanks.

(Meeting ended — transcript may be truncated; Fireflies sometimes ends early when everyone disconnects.)
